current_component_sources.quote: A more consequential opening has emerged in quantum memory. Building on an existing 3D passive-memory proposal, we have a candidate construction that replaces its higher-body interactions with local three-body qubit interactions while retaining long-lived thermal storage under a specified noise model. Two internal reviews have checked different parts of the argument and caught corrections that are being incorporated. If the full proof holds, this would make an abstract protected-memory design closer to the kinds of interactions hardware can implement. It is not yet a practical memory: the required temperature and interaction strengths may be extremely demanding, and efficient initialization and robustness to general hardware errors remain open. It has not had external review.

current_component_sources.quote: I’ve put the quantum-memory construction through a stricter resource check. The proof’s current sufficient temperature scale is extraordinarily small, and I cannot yet show how to load a qubit into the required thermal state efficiently. The very small bound is a conservative proof guarantee, not a demonstrated physical lower limit. So my assessment is: potentially meaningful mathematics about which interactions can retain a thermal memory, but not yet a credible practical memory breakthrough. The next attack is the actual write/loading operation and whether the resource bounds can be improved.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Complete candidate memory/resource update,approximately07:14 observation after07:05marker;partial reviews/corrections and loading obstruction retain source scope.

current_component_sources.quote: There’s a useful improvement to the quantum-memory route: a different three-body qubit construction has an internally checked energy-scale guarantee more than 100 million times larger than the first one. It uses more connections between the auxiliary qubits, so that gain has a hardware cost. The important caveat is that the actual memory temperature requirement is still much colder than that number alone suggests, and we still haven’t established efficient, fault-tolerant writing or robustness to general hardware noise. So I’m not yet calling it a practical memory.
